issues.issue: The cross-reference is to "Section XDI" (Section XIII), and the clause fixes a termination date of 05/13/2009 that does not match Item 2 of the original Declarations (04/13/2009). Which document fixes the true termination date, and hence when the Discovery Period begins, is open to construction.

The Discovery Period table sets a $160,000 retention for Directors and Officers Liability, which matches neither the $0 retention for Insuring Agreement (A) nor the $100,000 retention for Insuring Agreement (B) in Item 9 of the Declarations. Which retention governs a Discovery Period claim cannot be resolved from the two documents together.

"The acquiring entity" is not a defined term and "Financial Impairment" is defined in Section IV (I) only as a status of the Company, so the clause's exception is measured by a definition that on its face cannot apply to an acquirer. Whether the Insuring Agreement (B) retention attaches when the acquirer simply declines to indemnify is left open.

"The acquiring entity" is added to the definition of Company without being defined or identified anywhere in the Policy, and no test (asset purchase, merger, receivership sale) is given for who qualifies. The double limitation "only for Wrongful Acts involving the entity or entities set forth in Item 1" and "only for Wrongful Acts occurring prior to the termination date" further leaves the acquirer's status uncertain.

By making the acquiring entity part of the "Company," this amendment feeds directly into the Insured vs. Insured Exclusion in Section V (J), which bars Claims brought by or on behalf of the Company. Whether a suit by the acquirer or by a receiver standing in its place is thereby excluded is a conflict between this definition and Section V (J).

This states the Discovery Period premium is fully earned, while Section XIII (B)(2) obliges the Insurer to return 100% of unearned premium on Insurer cancellation. The two cannot both operate if the Insurer terminates coverage during the Discovery Period.

The Endorsement takes effect at 12:01 a.m. on 05/13/2009, the identical moment at which paragraph 1 of the same Endorsement terminates the Policy. Whether the Discovery Period begins before, at, or after termination is a question the two dates leave open.

This says nothing herein varies the Policy's terms, yet the same Endorsement deletes Section XII in its entirety and replaces the Section IV (E) definition of Company. The reach of the "other than as above stated" qualifier against those deletions is open to construction.

The notice states Defense Costs are included within the Limit of Liability, but Section XVI (K) says headings and descriptions form no part of the terms of coverage and this notice is not an operative provision. Whether the notice can be relied on as a term, alongside Section IX (A)(1), is arguable.

The Named Insured entry is garbled and partly illegible ("vant ederal Sa ares, Inc."), so the identity and order of the listed insured entities cannot be read off the face of the Declarations. Since Section IV (P) defines "Named Insured" as the first entity in Item 1, the defect matters.

The expiration date is printed as "0443/2009" and is superseded by the Amendment to Declarations extending the Policy Period to 05/13/2009. Which date governs "Policy Period" under Section IV (R) is not resolvable from Item 2 alone.

The $10,000,000 Total Policy Limit for all Insuring Agreements is stated against Item 8 limits that separately total $35,000,000, and Section VII (A)(1) and (A)(2) treat those limits differently. How the aggregate cap interacts with the individual limits is left to construction.

"If the eligibility requirements are met" identifies no requirements and points to no section, leaving the conditions for exercising the Discovery Period undefined in the Declarations. Section III supplies conditions but this Item does not incorporate them by reference.

Coverage is conditioned on a "Limit of Liability, retention and premium" being set forth, but Insuring Agreement (A) shows a retention of "N/A"/$0 and Agreements (A) and (B) share a single row. Whether the prerequisite is satisfied for Insuring Agreement (A) is arguable against Section I.

This says Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage, yet Endorsement 2949 adds a Securities Liability Exclusion to Section V and a separate Securities Liability Insuring Agreement (Form 5098) is issued. Whether securities claims fall under (C) or exclusively under the endorsement is a conflict between this note and those endorsements.

The Item fixes a $5,000 IRA/Keogh retention but then says that if IRA/Keogh coverage is provided by Endorsement the retention shall be that "set forth in Item 9," giving two different retentions for the same class of Claim. The cross-reference is also miscited as "Section ITV (X)(2)."

The list of incorporated Endorsements ends in illegible characters ("500! | 5 0€ > aH"), so which forms are incorporated cannot be determined from the text. The later Declarations amendments list a different set of forms (5081, 5082).

This makes the Declarations, Application, Policy and Endorsements the contract, while Section XVI (B) states that the Policy, Application and written Endorsements "constitute the entire agreement" without mentioning the Declarations. The two integration statements are not identical in scope.

This extends the Policy Period to 05/13/2009 while Item 2 of the original Declarations and the definitions of Policy Period and Policy Year in Section IV (R) and (S) key off the original 04/13/2009 expiration. Whether the extra month is a new Policy Year or part of the last one is a question the two provisions leave unresolved.

This Endorsement schedule (5081, 5082, 2223, 2949, 5091, 5093, 5098, TRIA-01, 8790D) differs from the schedules in Item 13 of the original Declarations and of the 2007 amendment. Which schedule identifies the forms actually incorporated is open to dispute.
The clause says nothing varies the Policy while the same Endorsement changes the Policy Period in Item 2. The scope of "other than as above stated" is the point of construction.

Vantus Bank is inserted as the first entity listed, which changes who the "Named Insured" is under Section IV (P) and therefore who may cancel, receive notice and act for all Insureds under Sections XIII (A) and XVI (D). Nothing in the Endorsement addresses that consequence.

This schedule omits form 5082 (the later Policy Period amendment) and differs from the schedules in the other two Item 13 provisions. Which endorsements are incorporated at which date is unresolved between them.
The preservation sentence sits in an Endorsement that in fact changes the Named Insured in Item 1. What "other than as above stated" preserves is arguable.

Coverage is withheld unless a Limit of Liability, retention AND premium are "set forth in the Declarations," but Item 6/9 show "$0" or "N/A" retention for Insuring Agreement (A) and no separate premium for Agreement (B). Whether those Agreements satisfy the tri-partite condition is a conflict with the Declarations table.

The carve-out "except for Loss the Company pays as indemnification" does not say what happens where the Company is legally permitted but unable to indemnify, a gap Section VII (B)(1) addresses differently. The phrase's boundary is the point of construction.

"Has agreed to or is legally permitted or required by law to indemnify" gives coverage on a permissive-indemnification basis without saying whether actual payment is required. Section VII (B)(2) treats permitted-but-unpaid indemnification as within Insuring Agreement (B), which sharpens the ambiguity.

This grant of Company liability coverage is cut back by the Securities Liability Exclusion added to Section V by Endorsement 2949, while Item 6 of the Declarations states that Insuring Agreement (C) includes Securities Liability coverage. The two cannot both be given effect.

The final sentence withholds coverage for "any loss arising from any act or omission by an Insured Person's estate, heirs, legal representatives, assigns, or spouse," which may take back the very coverage the subsection grants. Where the grant ends and the carve-out begins is unclear.

This coverage is deleted for the Brokerage/Advisory, Fiduciary and Securities Liability Insuring Agreements by paragraph 2.A of Endorsements 5091, 5093 and 5098. Whether any Not-for-Profit Directorship coverage survives across the Policy as a whole must be read from those endorsements.

The right to purchase is triggered by conversion only "subject to Section XIII (C)(1)(b)," but Section XIII (C)(2) says the occurrence of ANY of the conversion events in (C)(1) — including Financial Impairment under (C)(1)(a) — shall not affect the right to purchase the Discovery Period. The two provisions give different triggers.

The Discovery Period covers Wrongful Acts occurring before "the effective date of cancellation, nonrenewal or conversion," while the amended Section IV (E) in the Discovery Period Endorsement uses "prior to the termination date of this Policy" as its cut-off. Which date limits the covered Wrongful Acts is left unresolved.

The premium formula multiplies the Item 10(a) annual premium by the Item 4 percentage, but the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement instead sets out its own fixed premium figures per Insuring Agreement. Which controls if they diverge is not addressed.

The sixty-day lapse period runs from "the effective date of such cancellation, nonrenewal or conversion," but conversion under Section XIII (C) is an event with no stated effective date or notice. When the clock starts on a conversion is therefore uncertain.

The Discovery Period limit is made part of the immediately preceding Policy Year's Item 8 limit, yet the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement lists fresh per-Agreement limits ($10,000,000 D&O, $5,000,000 etc.) for the Discovery Period. Whether the Discovery Period has its own limits or shares the expiring year's is the conflict.

"Terms, conditions, Limits of Liability, retentions, or premiums different from those applicable to the expiring Policy" sets no ceiling, so any renewal offer however onerous defeats the Discovery Period right. The boundary of a qualifying "offer" is undefined.

"All applications, attachments and materials submitted to the Insurer" for this or any predecessor policy is unbounded, and it is not said what "materials" means or how far back "indirect renewal or replacement" reaches. That matters because Section XV makes those materials the basis of the Policy.

The definition sweeps in "economic advice, financial advice or investment advisory services" generally while carving out advice on "the FDIC-insured component of any deposit account," so the line between covered banking advice and excluded Brokerage/Advisory Services is indistinct. The same phrase drives the Section V (B) exclusion.

"A written or oral demand for monetary damages or non-monetary relief" has no threshold of formality, so whether a regulator's or receiver's demand letter or tolling request is a Claim (and when it was "first made") is open. The list is also confined to enumerated proceedings, which raises whether informal investigations qualify.

This definition is deleted and replaced by paragraph 4 of the Discovery Period Activation Endorsement, which substitutes a different definition including "the acquiring entity." Which definition of Company governs a Claim first made in the Discovery Period must be worked out between the two.

"Reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses" is not measured against any benchmark, and Section IX (B)(2) leaves the Insurer to evaluate reasonableness and necessity itself. What is reasonable and necessary is a standing point of construction.

The statute is misnamed as the "Employment Retirement Income Security Act" rather than the Employee Retirement Income Security Act. The mistake is mechanical but the term drives both the ERISA Exclusion and the Fiduciary Liability Insuring Agreement.

The definition excludes "a Leased Employee or Independent Contractor," capitalized as defined terms though neither is defined anywhere in Section IV. Who is excluded from "Employee," and therefore from "Insured Person," is left undetermined.

"Financial Impairment" is defined as a status "of the Company" but the enumerated triggers include the appointment of a receiver over "the Company or any Subsidiary," so it is unclear whether a Subsidiary receivership impairs the Company. The definition is applied elsewhere (Section VII (B), the Discovery Endorsement) to entities other than the Company.

This definition of Insured is deleted and replaced for Fiduciary Liability purposes by paragraph 2.C of Endorsement 5093, which adds Employee Benefit Plans. Which definition applies to a Claim implicating more than one Insuring Agreement is not addressed.
